(CNN) -- The European Union will launch its first naval operation Tuesday, protecting vessels from pirate attacks off the coast of Somalia, EU policy chief Javier Solana announced Monday. A French army helicopter taking off from French frigate Nivose,  on patrol in the Gulf of Aden. EU foreign ministers approved the mission during their regular meeting in Brussels on Monday. Solana said the operation is "very important" because EU vessels will be operating "in a place in the world that everybody's looking at because of the new problems related to piracy." "It's very important that we have taken that decision to launch it tomorrow," he added. The EU naval force will take over the role of escorting United Nations World Food Program vessels carrying food and relief supplies to war-torn Somalia, an EU news release said. Its mandate, which is spelled out in several U.N. Security Council resolutions, also will include "the protection of vulnerable vessels cruising off the Somali coast, and the deterrence, prevention and repression of acts of piracy and armed robbery off the Somali coast," the news release stated. The deployment follows a decision by the European Council in September that established a coordination cell that supported surveillance and protection operations by several member states off the Somali coast. Piracy has become increasingly common in that area this year, particularly in the Gulf of Aden. So far, pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels off Somalia's coast and successfully hijacked nearly 40, according to the International Maritime Bureau. Those hijacked vessels include an enormous oil tanker, a chemical tanker, and a ship laden with Soviet-era arms, including tanks. The pirates normally hold the ships for ransom. The Somali-based pirates have extended their reach beyond Somalia's coastline. On Saturday, a Dutch-operated container ship outran pirates off the coast of Tanzania, an IMB official told CNN. A luxury cruise ship carrying more than 1,000 passengers and crew successfully outran pirates off the coast of Yemen last weekend. A multinational fleet -- including vessels from the United States, NATO member states, Russia and India -- has been patrolling the Indian Ocean waters near the Gulf of Aden, which connects the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. Around 20,000 oil tankers, freighters and merchant vessels pass along the crucial shipping route each year. In a recent interview provided to CNN, a pirate leader claimed attacks on shipping would continue so long as life in Somalia remained desperate. "The pirates are living between life and death," said the pirate leader, identified by only one name, Boyah. "Who can stop them? Americans and British all put together cannot do anything."

This comprehensive approach reflects the EU's commitment to restoring security to one of the world's most dangerous maritime corridors.

The launch of this operation comes in response to a dramatic surge in piracy throughout the region this year. Pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels and successfully hijacked nearly 40 ships off Somalia's coast, creating serious concerns for international shipping and humanitarian operations alike.

Perhaps most troubling is the expanding scope of these criminal activities. Somali-based pirates have extended their reach well beyond Somalia's immediate coastline, demonstrating an alarming operational range. This growing threat was highlighted by a recent attack on a Dutch-operated container ship off the coast of Tanzania, illustrating that the danger now extends across a much broader stretch of the region's waters.

CNN, the Cable News Network, has long been one of the most recognizable names in global journalism. Since its founding in 1980, the American network has expanded far beyond its domestic roots, building a substantial presence across international markets—including the European continent.

## The Reach of CNN in Europe

The European audience has become an important part of CNN's global strategy. Through CNN International, the network delivers around-the-clock coverage of world events to viewers in the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, and many other European nations. Its London bureau serves as a major hub, coordinating reporting from across the region and providing a distinctly international perspective on breaking news.

The European media landscape is highly competitive, with established outlets such as the BBC, Euronews, and Sky News. # EU Launches First Naval Mission to Combat Somali Piracy

**Historic Operation Atalanta marks bloc's first-ever naval deployment**

The European Union has launched its first-ever naval operation, deploying warships to the waters off the coast of Somalia in an ambitious effort to combat the surge in piracy threatening one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

The mission, dubbed "Operation Atalanta," represents a significant step for the 27-member bloc, marking its first coordinated naval military engagement since the EU's founding.

## Protecting Vital Shipping Routes

The operation aims to protect commercial vessels and humanitarian aid shipments traveling through the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, where pirates have increasingly targeted ships for lucrative ransoms.

"This is a landmark moment for European security cooperation," an EU official said. "We are sending a clear message that the international community will not tolerate these attacks on innocent seafarers and vital commercial traffic."

The Gulf of Aden serves as a crucial gateway connecting Europe to Asia via the Suez Canal, with thousands of vessels passing through annually. The waters have become increasingly dangerous as pirate attacks have escalated in both frequency and boldness.

## A Growing Threat

Somali pirates, operating from the largely lawless coastline of the failed state, have captured numerous vessels and demanded millions of dollars in ransom payments. The hijackings have driven up shipping insurance costs and prompted some vessels to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding significant time and expense to voyages.

The pirates have grown increasingly sophisticated, using speedboats launched from larger "mother ships" to strike far from shore.

## International Response

The EU operation will coordinate with other naval forces already patrolling the region, including vessels from NATO and various individual nations that have dispatched warships to the troubled waters.

The mission's mandate includes protecting World Food Programme vessels delivering desperately needed humanitarian aid to Somalia, escorting commercial ships, and deterring pirate attacks through active patrols.

## Challenges Ahead

Despite the naval buildup, experts caution that military patrols alone may not solve the piracy problem, which is rooted in the poverty and instability plaguing Somalia after years of conflict and the absence of an effective central government.

The vast expanse of ocean that must be patrolled presents an enormous logistical challenge, with the area of operations spanning hundreds of thousands of square miles.

The operation reflects growing international concern over the pirate threat and represents a test of the European Union's ability to project military power and coordinate collective security operations beyond its borders.

---

# International Naval Coalition Confronts Persistent Somali Piracy Threat

*A look at the multinational efforts securing one of the world's most critical maritime corridors*

---

The waters off the Horn of Africa remain one of the maritime world's most closely watched regions, where an international coalition of naval forces continues efforts to protect commercial shipping and humanitarian aid deliveries from the threat of Somali piracy.

## The EU Naval Force: Operation Atalanta

At the center of international counter-piracy efforts stands the European Union Naval Force (EUNAVFOR) Somalia, better known as **Operation Atalanta**. Launched in December 2008 as the EU's first-ever naval operation, Atalanta was established in response to a dramatic surge in piracy that threatened one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

The operation's mandate encompasses several key objectives:

- Protecting vessels of the World Food Programme (WFP) and other humanitarian shipments
- Deterring and disrupting piracy and armed robbery at sea
- Protecting vulnerable commercial shipping
- Monitoring fishing activity off the Somali coast

Operating across a vast area encompassing the Gulf of Aden, the Somali Basin, and portions of the Indian Ocean, Atalanta coordinates warships, maritime patrol aircraft, and intelligence assets contributed by EU member states. The force works alongside other international naval presences, including NATO operations and the multinational Combined Task Force 151.

## Protecting Humanitarian Lifelines

Among the most vital functions of these naval operations is the protection of **World Food Programme vessels**. Somalia has long depended on humanitarian aid delivered by sea, with the WFP shipping food assistance to millions of vulnerable people across the region.

Before organized naval escorts began, these humanitarian shipments faced significant risk. Pirates recognized that hijacking a vessel—regardless of its cargo—could yield substantial ransoms. The introduction of dedicated naval escorts for WFP ships ensured that food aid could reach populations facing food insecurity without interruption.

The escort system typically involves naval vessels accompanying WFP-chartered ships through the most dangerous waters, providing armed protection from departure to safe arrival at Somali ports. This model has proven highly effective, with escorted humanitarian vessels maintaining a strong safety record.

## The Evolution of the Piracy Threat

Somali piracy reached its peak between 2008 and 2012, when hijackings became alarmingly frequent. At the height of the crisis, pirates held hundreds of hostages and dozens of vessels, extracting ransoms that reportedly totaled hundreds of millions of dollars.

The economic impact rippled across global trade. Shipping companies faced soaring insurance premiums, some vessels rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope at enormous additional cost, and the human toll on captured crews—often held for months in harsh conditions—drew international condemnation.

## A Combination of Countermeasures

The significant decline in successful piracy attacks resulted from multiple overlapping factors:

**Naval Presence:** The sustained multinational naval deployment created a deterrent effect and enabled rapid response to attacks in progress.

**Best Management Practices (BMP):** The shipping industry adopted standardized defensive measures, including increased speed through danger zones, the use of razor wire and water cannons, and the establishment of secure "citadels" where crews could shelter during an attack.

**Private Armed Security:** Many shipping companies began employing armed guards aboard vessels. Notably, no ship with an armed security team successfully aboard has been hijacked—a statistic that transformed industry practices.

**Regional Capacity Building:** International efforts also focused on strengthening regional maritime capabilities and addressing conditions ashore that contributed to piracy.

## Ongoing Vigilance Against Resurgence

Despite the dramatic reduction in attacks, security officials caution against complacency. The underlying conditions that fueled piracy—including instability in parts of Somalia, economic hardship, and illegal fishing that has depleted local resources—have not been fully resolved.

Periodic incidents serve as reminders that the threat persists. When naval patrols thin or when merchant vessels relax their defensive postures, opportunistic attacks can resurface. Maritime security analysts have documented occasional hijacking attempts and successful seizures in recent years, demonstrating that pirate networks retain the capability and intent to strike when opportunities arise.

Some incidents have involved the hijacking of smaller fishing vessels and dhows, which pirates sometimes use as "mother ships" to extend their range far into the Indian Ocean, launching attacks on larger commercial targets hundreds of miles from the coast.

## The Path Forward

The international counter-piracy effort off Somalia stands as a notable example of multinational cooperation, bringing together naval forces from Europe, Asia, North America, and beyond in pursuit of a common goal. Operation Atalanta has been extended multiple times, reflecting the recognition that maintaining maritime security requires sustained commitment.

Experts emphasize that lasting solutions extend beyond naval patrols. Addressing piracy's root causes—through economic development, governance improvements, and protection of Somalia's fishing waters from illegal exploitation—remains essential to preventing a resurgence.

For now, the combination of naval escorts, industry best practices, and international coordination continues to keep one of the world's most strategically vital waterways open—safeguarding both global commerce and the humanitarian aid upon which millions depend.

---

*This piece provides an overview of international maritime security efforts. Readers seeking current threat assessments should consult official maritime security advisories and organizations such as the International Maritime Organization.*

BRUSSELS (Wire) — The European Union launched its first-ever naval mission on Monday, dispatching warships to the Gulf of Aden to combat a surge in piracy off the coast of Somalia that has disrupted one of the world's busiest shipping lanes and driven up the cost of maritime insurance.

Javier Solana, the EU's foreign policy chief, announced the operation, codenamed Atalanta, saying the bloc had a duty to protect commercial vessels and safeguard humanitarian aid shipments bound for the Horn of Africa.

"The European Union is determined to play a full part in the fight against piracy and armed robbery off the Somali coast," Solana told reporters in Brussels. "This is a serious threat to international trade, to the freedom of navigation, and above all to the delivery of food aid to a population in desperate need."

The mission, drawing warships and surveillance aircraft from several member states, will escort vessels chartered by the World Food Programme and patrol shipping corridors where dozens of attacks have occurred this year. It marks a significant expansion of the EU's security ambitions, moving the bloc into naval operations for the first time.

Piracy off Somalia has escalated sharply, with attackers using speedboats launched from larger "mother ships" to seize vessels far out at sea. Maritime monitoring groups have logged roughly a hundred attacks this year, with dozens of ships hijacked and scores of crew members held hostage for ransom.

The seizures have grown increasingly audacious. Gunmen recently captured a Saudi supertanker laden with crude oil worth an estimated $100 million, holding it hundreds of miles offshore, and separately seized a cargo ship reportedly carrying battle tanks and other weaponry.

Ransom payments, often running into the millions of dollars, have made piracy one of the few lucrative enterprises in a country wracked by nearly two decades of conflict and without a functioning central government.

Reached by telephone in the coastal town of Eyl, a man who identified himself as a pirate holding a captured vessel was unrepentant. "The sea is our only livelihood," he said. "Foreign ships take our fish and dump their waste in our waters. We are not afraid of European warships — the ocean is very big, and we know it better than they do."

Analysts caution that a naval presence alone is unlikely to solve the problem, given the vast expanse of ocean to be patrolled and the instability on land that fuels the piracy. Solana acknowledged the challenge, describing the mission as one element of a broader international effort.

"There is no purely military solution," he said. "But we cannot stand by while these waters become lawless. This operation is a clear signal that the international community will act."

The operation is expected to run for an initial period of one year, with the possibility of extension.

# Multinational Naval Forces Intensify Anti-Piracy Operations in Gulf of Aden

**By Maritime Affairs Correspondent**

Naval forces from multiple nations continue coordinated patrols along one of the world's most strategically vital shipping corridors, responding to piracy threats that have periodically disrupted commerce off the Horn of Africa.

## A Critical Maritime Chokepoint

The Gulf of Aden connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean, serving as the primary passage for vessels traveling between Europe and Asia via the Suez Canal. Roughly 20,000 ships transit these waters annually, carrying oil, consumer goods, and raw materials worth billions of dollars.

The narrow waterway—bordered by Yemen to the north and Somalia to the south—creates natural bottlenecks where vessels slow their pace, historically making them vulnerable to attacks launched from small, fast skiffs.

## The Multinational Response

Several international coalitions have operated in the region over the years, including:

- **Combined Task Force 151**, a multinational naval effort established specifically for counter-piracy
- **Operation Atalanta**, the European Union's naval mission
- **NATO's Operation Ocean Shield** (concluded in 2016)

Warships from nations including the United States, China, India, Russia, Japan, and various European states have contributed vessels, creating an internationally recognized transit corridor where merchant ships can travel in protected convoys.

## Roots of the Problem

Analysts consistently trace Somali piracy to conditions ashore. Decades of state collapse, the absence of a functioning coast guard, illegal foreign fishing that depleted local waters, and widespread poverty created conditions where piracy became an attractive livelihood for young men in coastal communities.
